Port both copy-invariant tests (no BLE-only variant mentions a server or a restorable connection; every NOT-watching variant literally contains 'NOT watching' and never claims coverage) — extend the string set with the new iOS reasons and the tests cover them automatically. Render as a SwiftUI view with the error-container styling and an accessibility identifier standing in for the Compose testTag.

ports_cleanly.capability: Alerts screen (list, empty states, refresh, per-row ack)
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: SwiftUI `List`/`LazyVStack` keyed by serverId. `PullToRefreshBox` → `.refreshable { }`, applied ONLY when a backend is configured so backend-optional mode has no dead gesture (the modifier is conditional, which is the exact analog of omitting the wrapper). Empty-state pair selection ports verbatim, including ignoring `isLoading` in backend-optional mode. Severity colors move to an asset catalog with light/dark variants. Timestamp formatting (`Just now` / `Xm ago` / `Xh ago` / `MMM d, HH:mm`) via `RelativeDateTimeFormatter` and a locale-aware `Date.FormatStyle`. Snackbar → a bottom overlay shown once then cleared. Also fold in the stub `AlertHistoryScreen` — it renders a 'coming in Story 31.6' placeholder on Android and should simply not be ported.

ports_cleanly.capability: AlertsViewModel — state, backend-optional gating, honest error copy
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: An `@MainActor @Observable` model. `stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000))` → observation lifetimes tied to SwiftUI `.task`. Same pessimistic seeds (`backendConfigured` seeded false, floor status seeded from the provider's pessimistic `current()`). `refreshAlerts()` must still await the real backend-configured value off the stream rather than reading the pessimistic seed, and return silently when false. Same error mapping: `URLError` → "Can't reach your server — alerts may be out of date.", otherwise "Couldn't refresh alerts. Try again."; ack failures → "Acknowledged locally — will sync when reconnected." (transport/transient) vs "Couldn't sync this acknowledgment to the server." (terminal), silent in backend-optional mode. Unconditional local dedup-clear on ack ports as-is.

ports_cleanly.capability: Caregiver alerting (patient_name in title/slot/list, no_data data-gap special case, no client-side escalation)
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: Entirely server-driven, so it ports as data plumbing. `patientName` continues to feed the title suffix, the notification identifier (`alertType|patientName`, now a plain string so two patients naturally get distinct identifiers — no hash-collision risk), and the alert-card footer. `no_data` keeps its title special case (`<prefix>: No CGM data<suffix>`, never rendering the last-known value) and continues to route to the quiet informational tier — on iOS that is `interruptionLevel = .active`, the honest equivalent of IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT with no DND bypass. No client-side caregiver escalation, fan-out, or Telegram exists to port; keep the onboarding copy attributing those to the server and the watch copy stating caregiver/AI alerts need the backend.

ports_cleanly.capability: Alert notification rendering and actions (title format, body, tap target, only-alert-once behavior)
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: `UNMutableNotificationContent`: `title` from a pure `formatAlertTitle(alert:unit:)` port (EMERGENCY/URGENT/Warning/Info prefixes, ` - <patientName>` suffix, the `no_data` branch, and `GlucoseFormat.formatWithLabel` in the display unit while currentValue stays canonical mg/dL); `body` = the server message (iOS expands long bodies natively, so BigTextStyle needs no analog); `threadIdentifier = "com.glycemicgpt.ALERTS"` replaces setGroup; `categoryIdentifier` carries the 'Got It' action. `setOnlyAlertOnce(!isLow)` maps to: when re-posting the same identifier, set `sound = nil` and `interruptionLevel = .passive` for high/IoB updates, and keep the sound for lows so a life-threatening low re-alerts on every update. Fix the Android dead `navigate_to` extra properly: `didReceive` with the default action identifier must route to the Alerts tab, and `willPresent` MUST return `[.banner, .sound, .list]` — otherwise iOS silently swallows an urgent low while the app is in the foreground, which Android never does.

ports_cleanly.capability: Debug fault injection for alerting (simulate-backend-unreachable, fast staleness)
ports_cleanly.ios_approach: `#if DEBUG` is a strictly stronger gate than `BuildConfig.DEBUG` (the code is absent from the release binary). The OkHttp `SimulateUnreachableInterceptor` maps to a `URLProtocol` subclass registered on the session configuration, failing with `URLError(.notConnectedToInternet)` before the network on both the main and the stream sessions, and sitting below the reachability accounting so the injected failure trips the 2-consecutive-failure threshold exactly like a real one. Force-cancel the live stream when the toggle flips on. Fast staleness (20 s / 45 s) swaps the policy in the floor gate, the status pipeline, the tick cadence, and the wrist status timeout identically. These become MORE important on iOS than on Android: the Simulator has no Bluetooth at all, so this toggle plus a compile-time simulated pump/CGM source is the only way to exercise the floor during development.

needs_redesign.capability: SSE alert stream service (AlertStreamService) — a foreground service holding a long-lived server connection
needs_redesign.why: iOS has no foreground services. A background `URLSessionConfiguration` supports only discrete upload/download tasks and explicitly not `URLSessionDataTask` or streaming responses, and a suspended app has no runloop to receive events on. The stream can therefore only exist while the app process is actually running — foreground, or backgrounded but kept alive by Core Bluetooth activity. `foregroundServiceType="dataSync"`, START_STICKY, and the persistent notification have no analog whatsoever.
options: Keep SSE only while the process is alive (foreground plus BLE-kept-alive background), tear down cleanly on suspension, reconnect on resume, and let AlertStreamState sit at DISCONNECTED the rest of the time — which correctly arms the on-device floor via the existing degraded predicate.

Add APNs to the self-hosted backend and push each alert to the device. The wire slot already exists: `DeviceRegistrationRequest.platform` has an `ios` value in contract/openapi.json, and today `device_token` is only a locally generated UUID. Push is the only way a backend alert reaches a suspended or terminated app.

Poll `/api/v1/alerts/pending` from a `BGAppRefreshTask`. Opportunistic only: iOS decides when (typically no more often than ~15 minutes, often much less, never at all if the user rarely opens the app), so this is a backfill, never a delivery mechanism.
Use the SSE stream's absence as the only signal and rely entirely on the on-device floor for background coverage.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Ship option 1 + option 3 immediately (they need no backend change and preserve today's behavior whenever the app is alive), and treat option 2 as the delivery guarantee to add. All the hard parts of AlertStreamService port verbatim and should be kept: the connection-generation guard, the single-flight reconnect CAS, `min(1000 * 2^min(attempt,6), 60_000)` backoff, the 401/403 jump to `max(5, attempt)`, `STABLE_CONNECTION_MS = 10_000` before resetting backoff, the idempotent start, and reconcile-pending-acks on stream open. Keep readTimeout at 75 s (2.5 heartbeats) — its purpose, bounding how long a silently dead stream can look CONNECTED, is unchanged. Explicitly reject the two folk workarounds: a background-location or silent-audio keep-alive is an App Review 2.5.4 rejection ('background services only for their intended purposes'), and PushKit VoIP pushes have been unusable by non-VoIP apps since iOS 13 (the app is terminated if it does not report a call).

needs_redesign.capability: Notification channels, sounds, and versioning (three DND-bypassing channels, versioned ids, user-picked ringtone URIs)
needs_redesign.why: iOS has no notification channels, so the entire versioned-channel mechanism — and the `AlertSoundStore` channel-version keys, the `recreateChannel` dance, the legacy-channel deletion, and the documented non-atomic `incrementChannelVersion` bug — has no analog and simply disappears: sound and interruption level are per-notification-request properties, changeable at any time. What does not port is the sound source: iOS has no `RingtoneManager`, no system ringtone picker, and no way for a third-party app to read the system tone library or to play an arbitrary content URI as a notification sound. Custom sounds must be ≤30 s CAF/AIFF/WAV files resolvable by filename from the app bundle or the app container's `Library/Sounds`.
options: Curated set only: bundle a handful of alert sounds per category plus Default and (for the informational category only) Silent, mirroring today's picker shape without arbitrary URIs.

Curated set plus user import: a `UIDocumentPicker` / Files import that transcodes to ≤30 s CAF and writes into `<container>/Library/Sounds/`, which `UNNotificationSound(named:)` resolves — this restores genuine user choice.
Drop custom sounds entirely and use only the system default plus critical-alert sounds.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. Channel routing becomes per-request tiering with the SAME shared low/high type sets so a drifted `low_*` string is still the single point of failure to guard: low types → `interruptionLevel = .critical` when the entitlement is granted (falling back to `.timeSensitive`) with the low alert sound; high types → the same tier minus the low-specific repeat escalation; `iob_warning`, `no_data`, and every unknown type → `.active` with the default sound, which is the honest equivalent of routing to the IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT AI channel. Keep the Android rule that the informational category is the only one offering Silent, and keep hiding that picker row in backend-optional mode. Two behaviors must be stated in the PRD because they are not obvious: custom notification sounds are NOT applied to the notification when it is mirrored onto Apple Watch (watchOS plays its own default alert/haptic), so the sound choice is an iPhone-only feature; and a sound file longer than 30 s is silently replaced by the system default.

needs_redesign.capability: On-device alert floor — arming gates and firing (AlertFloor evaluation on every poll)
needs_redesign.why: Every decision in AlertFloor ports verbatim — the four gates, the classification order with urgent bands first, the inclusive boundaries, the 30-minute cooldown, the ack-gated episode guard against server history with its fail-toward-alerting exception handling and its `min(serverTs, now)` clamp, the local-floor entity shape and message copy, and the never-persist rule. What does not port is the execution model. On Android the floor is evaluated by a foreground service polling every 15 s forever. On iOS there is no such loop: the app must be resumed by the system to evaluate at all, and a suspended app cannot post a notification. The only reliable resume source for this app is Core Bluetooth (`bluetooth-central` background mode with `CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey` state restoration), which wakes the app on connect, disconnect, and characteristic-notification events. Compounding this, the pump drops idle BLE links at ~30 s and iOS will not run a 15 s timer while suspended, so the poll cadence itself is not under the app's control in the background.
options: Evaluate on every Core Bluetooth wake and accept whatever cadence the pump link produces, relying on the fact that the FRESH window is 6 minutes and therefore tolerant of a much slower cadence than 15 s.

Add a dead-man's-switch local notification: on every wake, cancel and re-schedule a local notification for now + the coverage window that says the phone has stopped watching. Silence then becomes an alarm, which is the only way iOS can surface 'the process died' without a process.
Move all alerting to APNs and drop the on-device floor — which forfeits the backend-optional mandate entirely.
Ask the user to keep the app in the foreground, which is not a product.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Options 1 and 2 together, and treat option 2 as the load-bearing part. Design the background link so that each pump behavior produces a wake: an idle disconnect at ~30 s is itself a `didDisconnectPeripheral` background wake, so a connect → poll → idle-disconnect → immediate re-`connect()` cycle becomes the de facto background cadence, with a pending `connect()` surviving suspension and even app relaunch under state restoration. That yields an effective evaluation interval well inside the 6-minute FRESH window while never requiring a background timer. Also persist the per-type cooldown and acked-type sets to the App Group so a background relaunch does not re-alarm an already-acknowledged low. Keep gate ordering exactly as Android has it — in particular, keep checking notification capability BEFORE stamping the cooldown.

needs_redesign.capability: Backgrounded coverage claim in the pump foreground notification (the only surface that speaks while the app is closed)
needs_redesign.why: iOS has no ongoing notification and no foreground service, so there is no notification whose mere presence proves a process is alive and whose text can be mutated from a background stream. Every iOS notification is user-dismissible and one-shot. The Android design leans on this surface precisely because it is the honest-coverage claim when the app is closed — the case iOS handles worst.
options: A Live Activity (ActivityKit) on the Lock Screen, Dynamic Island, and watchOS Smart Stack, updated from Core Bluetooth wakes, with `staleDate` set to the coverage expiry so the system itself renders a stale/unknown treatment with no code running.

A Lock Screen and Home Screen WidgetKit accessory widget whose timeline is built with pre-computed FUTURE entries — 'watching until T', then 'NOT watching' from T onward — so the claim decays exactly on time at zero refresh budget and while the app is dead.
A scheduled dead-man's-switch notification that fires if the app has not run in longer than the coverage window.
Accept that iOS has no always-visible surface and show the claim only in-app.
needs_redesign.recommendation: All three of options 1–3, because each covers a different failure mode: the Live Activity is the rich always-glanceable surface while the app is healthy, the widget is the surface that survives app death and decays honestly, and the notification is the only thing that can actively interrupt the user when nothing is running. State plainly in the PRD that a Live Activity runs at most about 8 hours active (roughly 12 hours visible after it ends) and that `Activity.request()` must be called from the foreground unless ActivityKit push-to-start over APNs is implemented — so it will lapse overnight and must be restarted on next foreground. Port the exact status→text mapping from PumpConnectionService (ServerActive / FloorWatching backend / FloorWatching BLE-only / NOT watching), keep the not-watching text reason-free on this surface as Android does, keep seeding from the pessimistic `current()` so a cold start into an existing outage never renders all-is-well copy, and keep the rule that a status-surface exception can never take down the BLE link.

needs_redesign.capability: AlertFloorStatusProvider — the single observation pipeline shared by all coverage surfaces
needs_redesign.why: The combine graph, the `staleAfterMs/4` tick clamped to [2 s, 30 s], the reactive threshold-configured input, `retryWhen` emitting a pessimistic snapshot rather than freezing, and the pessimistic `current()` seed all port cleanly to Combine or AsyncAlgorithms. The problem is its host: on Android it lives in a foreground service that never stops, so the claim provably decays. On iOS the pipeline only runs while the process runs, which means the very mechanism that makes the claim honest — recomputation on a ticker as reading age grows — stops exactly when the claim is most likely to be wrong.
options: Run the pipeline in the app process, accept that it stops, and let the in-app banner be the only surface that is truly live.

Make decay declarative: give every emitted `AlertFloorStatus` an explicit `validUntil` timestamp, and have each surface expire it without any running code — widget timeline entries scheduled at `validUntil`, Live Activity `staleDate = validUntil`, the watch's existing `receivedAtMs + timeoutMs` decay, and a dead-man's-switch notification scheduled for `validUntil`.
Fork the pipeline per surface so each can compute what it needs when it is asked.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2 built on top of option 1, and explicitly reject option 3 — the whole point of the Android design is that the in-app banner, the background surface, and the wrist can never disagree, and forking is the fastest way to reintroduce the lethal lie. Add `validUntil` as a first-class field on `AlertFloorStatus` so all four expiry mechanisms derive from one number, keep exactly one selector function, and keep the pessimistic `current()` seed (no CGM age, backendConfigured false) as the synchronous first frame.

needs_redesign.capability: Notification permission handling and the floor's dependency on it
needs_redesign.why: `NotificationManagerCompat.areNotificationsEnabled()` collapses to one boolean on Android. iOS has no single equivalent and, more importantly, has substantially more ways for a granted permission to still produce an inaudible alert — which directly threatens the honest-coverage invariant. `UNNotificationSettings` exposes `authorizationStatus`, `alertSetting`, `soundSetting`, `lockScreenSetting`, `criticalAlertSetting`, `timeSensitiveSetting`, and `scheduledDeliverySetting` (Notification Summary, which can batch a non-time-sensitive alert for hours). None of these is a single yes/no, and two decisive inputs — the ring/silent switch position and the current ringer volume — are not readable by any public API at all.
options: Port it as one boolean: `authorizationStatus == .authorized`, matching Android exactly and ignoring the rest.

Grade it: keep NOTIFICATIONS_DENIED as the highest-priority not-watching reason and add ALERTS_DISABLED, SOUND_DISABLED, CRITICAL_ALERTS_DENIED, TIME_SENSITIVE_DENIED, and SUMMARY_MAY_DELAY as additional reasons or as a separate 'watching, but you may not hear it' degraded tier.
Require critical alerts and refuse to claim coverage without them.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. Request `[.alert, .sound, .badge, .criticalAlert, .providesAppNotificationSettings]` at onboarding on BOTH the server and backend-optional paths, exactly as Android requests POST_NOTIFICATIONS on both, and never request `.provisional` (provisional authorization delivers quietly to Notification Center and would silently disable every alarm). Re-read `getNotificationSettings()` on every foreground, cache it, and feed it into the same status selector. `Settings.ACTION_APP_NOTIFICATION_SETTINGS` maps to `UIApplication.openSettingsURLString`. State the irreducible residual in the PRD: without the Critical Alerts entitlement, the app cannot detect a muted phone and therefore cannot honestly promise the alarm will be audible — that limit must be written into the copy, not hidden.

needs_redesign.capability: Watch alert relay (phone → wrist alert push) including setLocalOnly double-buzz avoidance
needs_redesign.why: Two separate problems. First, the transport: Google's DataClient with `setUrgent()` has no iOS equivalent with the same guarantees — `WCSession.sendMessage` requires both apps running and reachable, `updateApplicationContext` is latest-value-wins and drops payloads identical to the last (the Android design already defeats DataLayer dedup with a `_ts` key, which ports), and `transferUserInfo` queues reliably but is budgeted and gives no promptness guarantee. Second, and worse: `setLocalOnly` has NO iOS analog. iPhone notifications mirror automatically to a worn Apple Watch whenever the iPhone is locked, and there is no per-notification opt-out. The precise mechanism Android uses to guarantee 'a single fresh low is one wrist experience, not three' therefore does not exist.
options: Keep the custom relay and also let mirroring happen, accepting a double buzz whenever the phone is locked.
Drop the watch-local alert notification entirely and let system mirroring be the only wrist buzz, using WatchConnectivity purely to feed the watch's Alerts screen, complication, and coverage state.

Keep a watch-local notification only for the window mirroring does not cover (phone unlocked and actively in use, where Apple deliberately does not mirror) — which requires the watch to know the phone's lock state, which it cannot reliably do.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 2. It preserves the actual Android goal (one buzz per fresh low) using the platform's own mechanism, and it makes the floor-vs-server distinction irrelevant on the wrist rather than requiring a flag that does not exist. Keep the relay as a STATE channel: the 30-minute rebuzz window and the 5-minute silent refresh become state-push cadences that keep the watch's copy inside the 6-minute CGM stale band, not buzz decisions. Port the wrist-honesty invariants verbatim, because they are platform-independent and are the safety core of this capability: a non-alertable reading skips the WHOLE relay block (never a clear, because retracting a possibly-still-true low into 'All clear' off untrustworthy data is the worse lie), and clear is keyed on the classification being in range and never on a mapping-gap nil. Accept and document the honest consequence: when the iPhone is unlocked and in the user's hand, the watch will not buzz — which is the behavior every iOS user already expects from every app.

needs_redesign.capability: Wrist coverage mirror (monitoring status heartbeat) and the watch alert/complication surfaces
needs_redesign.why: The 3-minute status heartbeat is roughly 480 phone→watch transfers per day. No WatchConnectivity background delivery budget sustains that; the watch app would simply stop being woken, freezing exactly the surface whose purpose is to never freeze. Separately, the Android complication ports to a different technology: ClockKit complications are gone, replaced by WidgetKit accessory families (`accessoryCircular`, `accessoryCorner`, `accessoryInline`, `accessoryRectangular`) whose timelines are refresh-budget limited — a 15 s re-evaluation ticker is impossible for the complication (it is fine for the watch app's Alerts screen while it is frontmost).
options: Send status on change only via `updateApplicationContext`, piggyback it on the CGM payload already going to the watch, and lengthen the advertised timeout to match the real delivery cadence so the watch's local decay remains truthful.
Keep a heartbeat but at a much longer period (e.g. 15–30 minutes) and widen the advertised timeout correspondingly.
Drop the phone→watch status entirely and let the watch decay coverage off the CGM payload's own timestamp.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1. The watch-side half of this design is already exactly right for iOS and ports verbatim: the watch never re-derives coverage, it renders the phone's decision, stamps `receivedAtMs` on its own clock, decays after the advertised timeout, clamps that timeout into [10 s, 30 min], rejects unknown state strings, fails closed to NoRecentStatus on missing/aged/unknown/future-skewed status, and deliberately does not persist status across a watch process restart. Keep every one of those rules. For the complication, replace the 15 s ticker with pre-computed timeline entries — one entry now ('covered'), one entry at `validUntil` ('not covered') — which decays with zero refresh budget and no running code and is a strictly better fit than the Android design. Port the complication tint rules exactly, especially the rule that a stale alert may only render grey while something is watching (otherwise a dead phone behind a stale alert looks like a healthy all-clear). Port the watch Alerts screen states verbatim, including 'Not watching' with per-reason copy, 'Caregiver & AI alerts are paused — they need the backend.', 'No recent data', the TOO_STALE grey-out with 'as of Xm ago — data stale', and the amber 'Not watching — check your phone' overlay line.

needs_redesign.why: `WearableListenerService` has no iOS analog: a watchOS app cannot wake a suspended iPhone app on demand. `sendMessage` only works while the counterpart is running and reachable; `transferUserInfo` queues but delivers whenever the iPhone app next runs, which could be minutes.
options: `WCSession.sendMessage` with a reply handler — immediate and correct while the iPhone app is running, unavailable otherwise.
`transferUserInfo` — always eventually delivered, possibly late; acceptable because every local silencing effect happens on the phone anyway and the alert cannot re-fire once the row is marked.
Use the mirrored notification's own 'Got It' action: iOS routes an action taken on a mirrored notification back to the iPhone app and launches it in the background to handle it.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 3 as the primary path, with options 1 and 2 as the fallback for dismissing from the watch app's own Alerts screen. Option 3 is strictly better than what Android has and fixes a documented Android gap: the mirrored action carries the specific alert's identifier, so a wrist dismiss targets THAT alert rather than 'the newest unacknowledged server alert', and it can silence a device-computed floor alarm — which the Android wrist dismiss provably cannot, because floor alerts have no database row. Keep the ordering invariant: mark locally first, so the wrist's 'cleared' is truthful even when the backend is unreachable and the server sync defers to the reconcile pass.

needs_redesign.capability: Alerting lifecycle across app and device restarts (BootCompletedReceiver, service start on login/settings, self-stop on no session)
needs_redesign.why: iOS has no launch-on-boot for third-party apps under any entitlement, so `BootCompletedReceiver` has no analog. There are no services to start or stop, so 'start on login / start from settings init / stop on logout / self-stop when no session' collapses into ordinary object lifecycle. What replaces boot-start is far weaker and needs to be designed for explicitly.
options: Core Bluetooth state preservation and restoration: register the central manager with `CBCentralManagerOptionRestoreIdentifierKey`, implement `centralManager(_:willRestoreState:)`, and keep a pending `connect()` outstanding — iOS will relaunch the app into the background when the paired pump produces a matching event.
APNs: a user-visible push launches the app to run its notification-service extension and delivers the alert even from a terminated state.
Require the user to open the app after every reboot.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Options 1 and 2, and be blunt in the product about their limits rather than papering over them. Three facts must be surfaced in onboarding, in Settings, and in the coverage copy: nothing runs after a reboot until the user unlocks the phone at least once; if the user force-quits the app from the app switcher, ALL background relaunch — including Bluetooth state restoration and silent push — is disabled until they manually reopen it; and Low Power Mode disables background app refresh (it does not sever an established BLE link, but it removes the backfill path). Force-quit is the single most common way an iOS diabetes app goes silent, and the app should be able to detect a suspiciously long gap since its last run and say so on next launch.

impossible.capability: Raising the system alarm volume for a low alert and restoring it on acknowledge (boostAlarmVolume / restoreAlarmVolume over AudioManager.STREAM_ALARM, with the persisted saved-volume and retry-on-failed-restore)
impossible.why: iOS exposes no public API to set the output or ringer volume. `AVAudioSession` can read `outputVolume` but cannot set it; driving the `MPVolumeView` slider programmatically is a long-standing App Review rejection; and there is no per-stream volume model at all. There is also no public API to read the ring/silent switch position, so the app cannot even detect that the boost would have been needed.
impossible.closest_alternative: With the Critical Alerts entitlement, `UNNotificationSound.criticalSoundNamed(_:withAudioVolume:)` (or `defaultCriticalSound(withAudioVolume:)`) plays the alert at a caller-specified volume regardless of the ringer position, the silent switch, and Do Not Disturb. That replaces boost-and-restore entirely and is strictly better: no saved-volume state, no restore step on acknowledge, no risk of leaving the user's phone at maximum volume after a process death. Recast the Settings toggle 'Boost Volume for Lows' as 'Use Critical Alerts for lows' with a volume slider, and remove the restore step from the acknowledge ordering. Without the entitlement there is no alternative at all: an alert can never be louder than the user's current setting, and the app cannot tell that the phone is muted.

impossible.capability: Bypassing Do Not Disturb, Focus, and the silent switch by application decision (NotificationChannel.setBypassDnd(true) on the low and high glucose channels, backed by a normal install-time permission)
impossible.why: On Android this is free — declare ACCESS_NOTIFICATION_POLICY and set the flag. On iOS the equivalent is `interruptionLevel = .critical`, which requires the `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts` entitlement. That entitlement cannot be self-granted: it is issued only after Apple manually reviews a request form, is limited to medical, health, and public-safety apps, is bound to the App ID's provisioning profile, and can be declined. Even when granted, the user must separately allow Critical Alerts at the authorization prompt and can revoke it in Settings.
impossible.closest_alternative: `interruptionLevel = .timeSensitive` with the Time Sensitive Notifications capability, which any developer can enable in Xcode without Apple's approval. It breaks through Focus modes when the user permits it and bypasses the Notification Summary, but it does NOT override the silent switch, does NOT override Do Not Disturb when the app is not allowed, and does NOT raise the volume. Apply for the critical-alerts entitlement on day one, ship a build that degrades cleanly to `.timeSensitive`, and make the difference visible in the coverage copy. One trap to state explicitly: the iOS Simulator does not validate entitlements, so a locally added critical-alerts entitlement will appear to work in the Simulator and then silently fail on a real device — Simulator behavior is not evidence here.

impossible.capability: Custom per-alert vibration patterns (the low channel's [0, 500, 200, 500, 200, 500] waveform, and the watch's urgent waveform [0, 500, 200, 500] versus a 300 ms one-shot)
impossible.why: No public API on iOS or watchOS attaches a vibration waveform to a notification. Haptics for delivered notifications are chosen entirely by the system from the interruption level and the sound. `CoreHaptics` and `WKInterfaceDevice.play(_:)` only run while the app is executing and frontmost, which is precisely the case that alerting is not. The private `AudioServicesPlaySystemSoundWithVibration` vibration-pattern route is a rejection.
impossible.closest_alternative: Encode severity in the SOUND rather than the haptic — a distinctive custom sound per severity — and use `.critical` for lows so the system plays its strongest alert pattern. Make the urgency temporal instead of haptic: a bounded ladder of repeated notifications (for example every 2 minutes, capped, well inside the 64 pending-request limit) cancelled the instant the user acknowledges. That also recovers the intent behind Android's `setOnlyAlertOnce(false)` for lows. On the watch, the Android `showAlert` watch-face config that gates vibration has no analog and should become a per-severity notification setting in the watch app.

impossible.capability: Automatically restarting alerting after a device reboot (BootCompletedReceiver restarting AlertStreamService and PumpConnectionService on ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED)
impossible.why: iOS provides no launch-on-boot mechanism to third-party apps under any entitlement, background mode, or provisioning profile. There is no analog to RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED.
impossible.closest_alternative: Core Bluetooth state preservation and restoration will relaunch the app into the background when the paired pump produces a matching BLE event — but only after the user has unlocked the device at least once since boot, and never if the app was force-quit from the app switcher. A user-visible APNs alert will also launch the app. Neither is deterministic and neither can be relied upon as a coverage guarantee. The honest product answer is a Lock Screen widget and a scheduled dead-man's-switch notification that make the gap visible, plus explicit onboarding copy about reboot and force-quit.

impossible.capability: An ongoing, non-dismissible, indefinitely persistent status notification whose presence proves the monitor is alive (the pump foreground-service notification, NOTIFICATION_ID 1, mutated with the coverage claim)
impossible.why: Every iOS notification is user-dismissible and one-shot; there is no ongoing flag, no foreground-service notification, and therefore no notification whose existence is evidence that a process is running. The closest primitive, a Live Activity, is time-limited by the system (roughly 8 hours active and about 12 hours visible), can normally only be started while the app is in the foreground unless ActivityKit push-to-start over APNs is implemented, and is user-dismissible.
impossible.closest_alternative: A three-part composite: a Live Activity for the rich glanceable claim while the app is healthy; a Lock Screen and Home Screen WidgetKit accessory widget whose timeline contains a pre-computed future entry that flips the claim to NOT-watching at the exact expiry instant, so it decays correctly with the app dead and at zero refresh budget; and a scheduled dead-man's-switch notification that actively interrupts the user if the app has not run within the coverage window. The PRD must state plainly that iOS cannot guarantee a permanently visible 'we are watching' indicator — the Live Activity will lapse overnight and must be restarted on next foreground.

impossible.capability: Holding a long-lived server connection (the SSE alert stream) open while the app is suspended or terminated
impossible.why: A background `URLSessionConfiguration` supports only discrete upload and download tasks; `URLSessionDataTask` and streaming responses are explicitly unsupported on background sessions, and a suspended app has no runloop on which to receive events. There is no background mode that grants a third-party app persistent network execution. This is the mechanism, not merely the timing: it is why AlertStreamService as designed cannot exist on iOS.
impossible.closest_alternative: APNs is the only path by which a server-originated alert reaches a suspended or terminated iOS app. The backend already models this — `DeviceRegistrationRequest.platform` includes an `ios` value — and today's `device_token` is only a locally generated UUID, so the wire slot exists but the sender does not. Retain the SSE client for low-latency delivery and for its liveness signal while the process is alive (foreground, or backgrounded and kept alive by Core Bluetooth), and let the existing degraded predicate arm the on-device floor for every other moment.

impossible.capability: A custom watch face carrying glucose and alert state, and a watch-face configuration flag gating alert vibration (the `watchface` Wear OS module and its `showAlert` config)
impossible.why: watchOS does not permit third-party watch faces. There is no API, no entitlement, and no review path — Apple has never opened watch faces to developers. The Wear OS `watchface` module (digitalFull and analogMechanical variants) has no analog whatsoever, and neither does a watch-face-level configuration that the alert code reads.
impossible.closest_alternative: WidgetKit accessory complications that the user places on Apple's built-in faces (accessoryCircular, accessoryCorner, accessoryInline, accessoryRectangular), a Smart Stack widget, and Live Activities surfaced in the watchOS Smart Stack. The `showAlert` gate becomes an ordinary per-severity setting inside the watch app rather than a watch-face property. Expect the visual identity of the Wear OS faces to be unshippable and plan for complication-only branding.

ios_requirements: The system must deliver audible glucose alerts for urgent low, low, high, urgent high, and insulin-on-board conditions received from a paired self-hosted backend, using the exact server alert-type vocabulary (low_urgent, low_warning, high_warning, high_urgent, iob_warning) and tolerating unrecognized future types by delivering them at the informational tier rather than dropping them.

The system must run with no backend configured at all and still raise on-device low and high alarms computed on the iPhone from the most recent pump CGM reading, threshold-only, with no trajectory projection, no prediction horizon, and no insulin-on-board escalation, and the alert body must state that provenance and its limits.

The system must never raise an on-device alarm from a CGM reading whose own sensor timestamp is more than 6 minutes old, must never raise one from a reading dated more than 60 seconds in the future, and must suppress all on-device alarming while the device wall clock is running more than 60 seconds behind the highest time the app has previously observed.
The system must never raise an on-device alarm from thresholds that neither the user nor their server has explicitly set; built-in default values must never arm the alarm.

The system must let a user set four alert thresholds (urgent low, low, high, urgent high) on the device when no backend is configured, entering them in their displayed unit, rejecting any value outside 20-500 mg/dL and any ordering other than urgent low ≤ low < high ≤ urgent high, and persisting nothing at all when validation fails.

The system must present thresholds as read-only with an explanation that they are edited in the web app whenever a backend is configured, and must adopt a server-side threshold change within one hour without the user opening the app, whenever the app has any opportunity to run in that hour.

The system must silently discard a server threshold response that fails validation, leaving the last known good values in place, and must never clamp an out-of-range or misordered server value into range.
The system must preserve device-set thresholds across sign-out, and must discard server-set thresholds on sign-out or when the user removes the server URL.

The system must deliver an urgent low alert so that the user hears it while the phone is in a Focus mode, in Do Not Disturb, or muted, wherever the platform permits, and must state in plain language, in the app and in the coverage claim, when it cannot make that guarantee.

The system must let a user choose a distinct alert sound per severity tier from a bundled set, import their own audio file as an alert sound, and select silence for the informational (AI / data-gap) tier only.
The system must repeat an unacknowledged urgent alert on a bounded, finite schedule until acknowledged, and must stop repeating immediately when the user acknowledges.
The system must display an alert while the app is in the foreground — a foreground app must never silently swallow an urgent low.

The system must let a user acknowledge an alert directly from the notification on iPhone or on Apple Watch without opening the app, and every local silencing effect — dismissing the notification, cancelling the repeat schedule, clearing the duplicate-suppression record — must take effect regardless of whether the server is reachable or responsive.

An acknowledgment made while offline must never be reversed by a later server delivery of the same alert, and must sync to the server automatically when connectivity returns without the user retrying.

The system must not re-alarm the same alert type more than once per 30 minutes while it remains unacknowledged, must re-alarm exactly 30 minutes after an acknowledgment if the condition still persists, and must alarm immediately as a new episode if the value recovers and then re-crosses.
The system must not re-alarm on the device for a condition the server already announced and the user has not yet acknowledged, using the server alert history to seed the suppression window.

The system must tell the user at all times, on every surface it offers — in-app, Lock Screen, and Apple Watch — whether anything is currently watching for lows and highs, and must never claim coverage it cannot deliver.
Every coverage claim must carry an explicit expiry time and must degrade to an unknown or not-watching state at that time without the app running.

The system must give a specific, actionable reason whenever it is not watching, drawn from: notifications denied, alerts disabled, alert sound disabled, critical alerts denied, time-sensitive alerts denied, notification summary may delay alerts, thresholds not configured, thresholds not yet synced from the server, no pump connection, no recent glucose reading, or coverage expired — presenting the most actionable reason when several apply.
The system must proactively notify the user when it has stopped watching for longer than the coverage window, even though no application code is executing at that moment.

The system must warn the user, during onboarding and in settings, that force-quitting the app from the app switcher, or not unlocking the phone after a restart, disables all background alerting until the app is reopened, and must detect and report a suspiciously long gap since it last ran.
The system must resume alerting automatically after a background termination when the paired pump produces a Bluetooth event, without any user action.

The Apple Watch app must show the current alert, its age computed on the watch's own clock, and whether the iPhone is currently watching; it must visually grey an alert whose underlying data has become too stale, and must show a 'no recent status' state rather than 'all clear' when it has not heard from the iPhone within the advertised window.

The Apple Watch must never independently conclude that coverage is healthy — it must render the iPhone's claim, decay it locally, and fail closed on any missing, aged, future-dated, or unrecognized status.

A watch complication must reflect alert and coverage state on the watch face and must change to a not-covered appearance at the coverage expiry time without requiring the iPhone or either app to be running.
A single fresh low must produce one wrist alert experience, not several.

The system must never retract a wrist alert into an 'all clear' state on the basis of a reading it cannot vouch for; when the underlying reading is not trustworthy it must leave the wrist alert standing and let it age out.

The system must show the most recent 100 server alerts, prune alerts older than 7 days, offer pull-to-refresh only when a backend is configured, and explain in backend-optional mode that on-device alarms appear as notifications rather than in the history list.

The system must render every glucose value in the user's chosen display unit while storing and transmitting canonical mg/dL, converting exactly once with the single constant 18.0156 and rounding last.
A caregiver data-gap alert must never display a glucose value in its title, because that value is only a last-known reading during the very blackout being reported.
Tapping an alert notification must open the app to the Alerts screen.

The system must, in developer builds only, let the developer inject simulated CGM readings, force the backend unreachable, and compress the staleness policy to seconds, so that every alerting path — floor arming, floor firing, cooldown, episode guard, coverage decay, and wrist mirroring — is exercisable in the iOS Simulator without a physical pump or a live server.

The system must keep its alert database and stored credentials readable while the device is locked after first unlock, so that background alerting, acknowledgment, and duplicate suppression work on a locked phone.

The freshness policy, threshold bounds and ordering rule, unit conversion constant, re-alarm cooldown, coverage timeout, and alert-type vocabulary must have exactly one definition, shared by the iPhone app, the Apple Watch app, and every widget and extension.

risks.risk: There is no background execution guarantee on iOS. The on-device alert floor only evaluates when the system resumes the app, and a suspended app cannot post a notification at all. The Android design's core promise — that the phone is a backstop when the server cannot deliver — becomes conditional on the pump's Bluetooth link generating wake events. If the link drops and does not reconnect, the app goes silent with no mechanism to notice from the inside.
risks.mitigation: Make silence itself alarm: on every wake, cancel and re-schedule a dead-man's-switch local notification for now plus the coverage window. Pair it with a Lock Screen widget whose timeline contains a pre-computed future entry that flips to NOT-watching at the same instant, so the claim decays with zero code running. Design the BLE link so every pump behavior — including the ~30 s idle disconnect — produces a background wake, and keep a pending connect() outstanding at all times so state restoration can relaunch the app.

risks.risk: The Critical Alerts entitlement is granted only by Apple's manual review and may be declined. Without it the app cannot bypass Do Not Disturb, cannot override the silent switch, cannot raise the volume, and cannot even detect that the phone is muted. Android gets all of this from a normal install-time permission. A denied entitlement means an urgent low can be delivered perfectly and heard by nobody.
risks.mitigation: Apply on day one and treat it as a project-schedule dependency, not a late polish item. Ship a build that degrades to interruptionLevel .timeSensitive (freely available, breaks through Focus and the Notification Summary) and make the difference explicit in the coverage copy rather than hiding it. Design the coverage claim so the entitlement state is one of its inputs from the start, so lighting it up later is a data change and not a redesign.

risks.risk: Force-quitting the app from the app switcher permanently disables ALL background relaunch on iOS — Bluetooth state restoration and silent push included — until the user manually reopens it. So does never unlocking the phone after a reboot. Both are invisible to the app while they are happening and are the most common way iOS diabetes apps go silent.
risks.mitigation: Persist a last-ran timestamp on every wake and, on next launch, detect and prominently report the gap. Surface the force-quit warning in onboarding and in Settings. Use the Lock Screen widget's scheduled expiry entry as the surface that stays honest through the dead window, since it needs no running process.

risks.risk: Backend-originated alerts cannot reach a suspended or terminated iOS app at all without APNs, and adding APNs to a self-hosted backend has an unresolved trust and key-distribution problem: the APNs auth key is issued to the app's Apple Developer Team and scoped to the bundle ID, so a self-hoster cannot obtain one for someone else's app. Today the Android app has no push path whatsoever and treats device_token as a local UUID.
risks.mitigation: Ship first with SSE-while-alive plus the on-device floor plus opportunistic BGAppRefresh pulls, and be explicit in the coverage copy that backend alerts do not arrive while the app is not running. Resolve the push architecture as a separate product decision (see questions); the openapi contract already reserves platform: ios on device registration, so the wire is not the blocker.

risks.risk: The pump drops idle BLE links at approximately 30 seconds and the Android design keeps them alive with a 15-second poll driven by a foreground service and a wake lock. iOS will not run a background timer, so the poll cadence in the background is dictated by Bluetooth events. The likely result is a connect / poll / idle-disconnect / reconnect cycle with a re-authentication (JPAKE) on every reconnect — battery cost, more failure surface, and occasional gaps that could push the newest reading past the 6-minute FRESH window and silently disarm the floor.
risks.mitigation: Verify early whether the pump can be configured to push characteristic notifications rather than requiring host-initiated polls, since a notifying peripheral wakes the app for free. Measure the real background reconnect cadence and re-authentication cost on a device before committing to the freshness constants. If the achievable cadence approaches the 6-minute window, that is a coverage fact that must be surfaced, not tuned away by widening the window.

risks.risk: The developer's stated validation loop — both apps in the iOS Simulator — is blind to nearly every high-severity failure mode in this subsystem. The Simulator has no Core Bluetooth at all (CBCentralManager reports .unsupported), does not faithfully simulate suspension, termination, or BLE state restoration, has no Focus modes, no Do Not Disturb, no ring/silent switch, and no real WatchConnectivity delivery budgets. Local notifications and simctl push do work, and Live Activities and the Dynamic Island do render, so the Simulator will happily demonstrate a version of the feature that behaves completely differently on a device.
risks.mitigation: Build a compile-time simulated pump/CGM source and a debug reading injector as first-class, day-one deliverables (the Android repo already has the inject seam to mirror), and pair them with the fast-staleness policy so freshness transitions play out in seconds. Treat Simulator success as a logic test only. Gate every release on an on-device smoke suite that exercises: locked-phone alert delivery, Focus and Do Not Disturb behavior, force-quit recovery, post-reboot behavior, background BLE reconnect cadence, and a real iPhone-to-Watch pair.

risks.risk: The iOS Simulator does not validate entitlements. A locally added critical-alerts entitlement will appear to work in the Simulator — the authorization prompt shows the Critical Alerts option and the notification behaves as if granted — and will then fail silently on a real device without Apple's grant. This is a false positive on the single most safety-critical delivery property.
risks.mitigation: Never accept Simulator behavior as evidence for critical alerts. Add a runtime assertion that reads UNNotificationSettings.criticalAlertSetting on a real device and feeds it into the coverage claim, and put an on-device critical-alert delivery check in the release smoke suite.

risks.risk: iOS has more ways for a granted notification permission to still be inaudible than Android does, and two of them — the ring/silent switch position and the current ringer volume — are unreadable by any public API. The Notification Summary (scheduled delivery) can batch a non-time-sensitive alert for hours. The honest-coverage invariant that this whole subsystem is built around therefore has an irreducible blind spot on iOS.
risks.mitigation: Read the full UNNotificationSettings on every foreground and feed alertSetting, soundSetting, lockScreenSetting, criticalAlertSetting, timeSensitiveSetting, and scheduledDeliverySetting into the status selector as distinct reasons. Always mark glucose alerts .timeSensitive at minimum so they escape the Summary. Write the residual blind spot into the coverage copy rather than claiming a guarantee that cannot be verified.

risks.risk: Using NSFileProtectionComplete on the alert database or kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlocked on the refresh token would render both unreadable while the phone is locked — which is precisely when a background alert arrives, when the episode guard needs to read server history, and when an acknowledgment from a mirrored notification needs to write. The failure would be silent and would appear only on a locked device, which the Simulator never truly reproduces.
risks.mitigation: Pin the database to NSFileProtectionCompleteUntilFirstUserAuthentication (the platform default — the risk is an over-eager hardening pass raising it) and the token Keychain items to kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly. Add a locked-device test to the on-device smoke suite. If SQLCipher is added on top, declare it in ITSAppUsesNonExemptEncryption for App Store Connect.

risks.risk: The wrist coverage heartbeat as designed — every 3 minutes, roughly 480 phone-to-watch deliveries per day — exceeds any WatchConnectivity background budget. The watch app would stop being woken and the coverage mirror would freeze, which is exactly the failure the heartbeat exists to prevent.
risks.mitigation: Move to on-change delivery via updateApplicationContext (with a timestamp field to defeat latest-value dedup, as the Android design already does for DataLayer), piggyback on the CGM payload already being sent, and lengthen the advertised timeout to match the real delivery cadence so the watch's existing local decay stays truthful. The watch already decays off receivedAt plus timeout and fails closed — that half needs no change.

risks.risk: A Live Activity is capped by the system at roughly 8 hours active and about 12 hours visible, and normally can only be started from the foreground. The always-glanceable coverage surface will therefore vanish overnight — during the exact hours when an unattended low alarm matters most — unless the user opens the app.
risks.mitigation: Do not make the Live Activity the sole background surface. Carry the Lock Screen widget (which has no lifetime cap and decays via pre-scheduled timeline entries) and the dead-man's-switch notification as the durable surfaces, and treat the Live Activity as enrichment. If push is added later, ActivityKit push-to-start restores the ability to revive it without user action.

risks.risk: The floor's per-type cooldown and acknowledged-type state is in-memory only. Android tolerates that because the hosting foreground service rarely dies; iOS kills the process far more aggressively, so a background relaunch would re-alarm a low the user already acknowledged — the exact alarm-fatigue failure the 30-minute window exists to prevent, and the one the design says trains users to disable notifications.
risks.mitigation: Persist lastFiredAtByType and ackedTypes to the App Group defaults on every mutation, with the same monotonic and clamping rules. This is a small, safe improvement over the Android behavior and costs nothing.

risks.risk: TestFlight distribution constrains the release cadence and the review posture: builds expire after 90 days, external testing requires Beta App Review, and a glucose-alerting app draws scrutiny under the physical-harm guideline. A critical-alerts entitlement request attached to an open-source, individually distributed medical-adjacent app may stall or be declined, which would gate the alerting story rather than a shipping detail.
risks.mitigation: Keep the read-only, monitoring-only architecture front and centre in the review submission and surface the existing MEDICAL-DISCLAIMER copy prominently in-app and in the TestFlight description, matching the posture that comparable open-source diabetes clients ship under. Decouple the entitlement from the release plan by making the .timeSensitive fallback a fully supported, honestly labelled configuration rather than a stopgap.

questions_for_pm: Push delivery is the only way a backend alert reaches a suspended or terminated iOS app, but the APNs auth key is issued to the app's Apple Developer Team and scoped to its bundle ID — a self-hoster cannot obtain one. That leaves three mutually exclusive product postures, and the choice is a trust and privacy decision, not a technical one: (a) no push at all, so backend alerts only arrive while the app is running and the on-device floor covers everything else — self-hosting stays pure but iOS backend alerting is materially weaker than Android's; (b) the project operates a central push relay that self-hosted servers call, which means alert metadata transits infrastructure the user does not control; or (c) the project distributes its APNs key to self-hosters, which lets any key holder push notifications to every user of the app. Which posture do we take?

When the app cannot verify that an alarm will actually be audible — no Critical Alerts entitlement, so the ring/silent switch and volume are unreadable by any API — does the coverage claim say 'watching' or does it say 'watching, but you may not hear it'? The strict reading of the honest-coverage principle argues for the caveat, but it would appear for nearly every user nearly all the time, which risks training people to ignore the one surface whose entire purpose is to be believed. Android never faced this because DND bypass is free there.
